clue.text: These youngsters could be seconds late

indicators.note: says the letters of the words that follow could be rearranged into something else

explanation.surface: A complaint that teenagers are always a few moments behind time.
explanation.definitionFit: Teenagers are young people in the stage between childhood and adulthood.

clue.text: Missionary who can handle a spoon?

explanation.surface: A preacher abroad who is handy with cutlery.
explanation.walkthrough: Apostle spoons are old silver spoons whose handles end in the figure of one of Christ's twelve followers, so such a figure literally is the handle.
explanation.definitionFit: The first followers of Christ were sent out to preach, and the carved figure forms the handle of a traditional christening spoon.

clue.text: The Ring done badly for the cinema

parts.note: a ring is round, the shape of the letter O

indicators.note: the word done is treated badly, its letters knocked out of order

explanation.surface: Wagner's Ring cycle performed so poorly it might as well be at the pictures.
explanation.definitionFit: Odeon is a well-known chain of British picture houses, used generically for a movie theatre.

clue.text: Danger-set at odds-set at odds?

indicators.note: letters that are at odds with one another are in disarray, so the hyphenated word is rearranged

explanation.surface: A playful repetition, as if a dangerous situation leaves people quarrelling.
explanation.walkthrough: The same phrase 'at odds' serves twice: first as the anagram signal on DANGERSET, then within the definition 'set at odds'.
explanation.definitionFit: People who have become alienated from each other are divided and unfriendly.

clue.text: Comb for Denry Machin?

explanation.surface: Asking what grooming tool suits a character from a novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Denry Machin is the hero of Arnold Bennett's novel The Card, an English Potteries tale of a cheeky go-getter; to card wool is to comb it.
explanation.definitionFit: Carding is combing raw fibres straight, and a cheeky, amusing fellow is called a card, as Bennett's hero is.

clue.text: We would support Elwyn Wild as a groom, say

indicators.note: in a down answer the supporting piece sits beneath the other one
the name Elwyn goes wild, its letters scattered into a new order

parts.note: we would contracts to we'd

explanation.surface: Someone backing a man named Elwyn Wild on his wedding day.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down answer WED sits beneath, so supports, NEWLY, the reshuffled ELWYN.
explanation.definitionFit: A bridegroom is a man just married or about to be, an example of the newly married.

clue.text: This photograph is religious in the main

indicators.note: the pious piece is set in the middle of the word for the ocean

parts.note: the main is a poetic term for the open sea
pi is slang for pious or religious

explanation.surface: A picture of something devout out on the ocean.
explanation.definitionFit: An old brownish-toned print takes its name from the cuttlefish ink once used as a pigment.

clue.text: Odd English in dry situation makes for shakiness

definitions.note: the noun stands loosely for the adjective; the clue says the answer makes for it

indicators.note: the odd English pair goes in the middle of the word dry

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A strange Englishman stuck somewhere arid ends up trembling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'makes for' links wordplay to definition: the answer describes what produces shakiness, which is why an adjective is defined by a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone tottery and trembling from age is unsteady on their feet.

clue.text: Disobedient Christian, for example?

parts.note: not a wayward believer but Fletcher Christian, who led the rebellion on HMS Bounty in 1789

explanation.surface: A believer who refuses to follow the rules of the faith.
explanation.definitionFit: Fletcher Christian led the crew who seized the ship from Captain Bligh, the classic seaborne rebel.

clue.text: The one fielding lapse that brings defeat

explanation.surface: A cricket blunder in the field costs the match.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a fielder's wild return that runs past the stumps gives away extra runs; it is called by this name.
explanation.definitionFit: A wayward return throw in cricket is a fielding error, and to topple or defeat a ruler is to bring them down.

clue.text: Beat poet?

explanation.surface: Asking whether a writer belongs to the Beat Generation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beat poet' suggests Kerouac and Ginsberg, but the clue splits into a verb and a separate poet, Ezra Pound.
explanation.definitionFit: To strike repeatedly is to hammer away, and Ezra Pound was an American modernist poet.

clue.text: At home in that military helmet

indicators.note: the at-home piece is placed in the middle of the word that

parts.note: taken as written
in is a standard synonym for at home

explanation.surface: A soldier's headgear kept at the house.
explanation.definitionFit: Soldiers' steel helmets were nicknamed after the metal they seemed made of.

clue.text: Timed any to go off?

indicators.note: letters going off like a blast end up scattered in a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Asking whether some timed device has been set to explode.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both an anagram of TIMEDANY and a description of a bomb set on a timer.
explanation.definitionFit: Nobel's high explosive is what a timer would be set to detonate.

clue.text: Bind book

explanation.surface: Two plain words placed side by side, like a bookbinder's sign.
explanation.definitionFit: To commit someone by a promise is to bind them, and to reserve or hire a performer is to book them.

clue.text: Girl's first at school, taking a gander

indicators.note: the first letter of the possessive word is taken

parts.note: Lancing College is an English public school in West Sussex

explanation.surface: A schoolgirl who is first in her class having a quick look.
explanation.walkthrough: Lancing is an English boarding school; 'gander' here is the slang for a look, not a goose.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking a quick look is having a peek, as a gander is slang for one.

clue.text: Engineers wearing best clothes in the sugar factory

indicators.note: the engineers come first, putting on the fancy clothes that follow them

parts.note: RE is the Royal Engineers, the British Army's engineering corps
finery is one's best clothes

explanation.surface: Army engineers dressed up for a visit to a sugar works.
explanation.definitionFit: Raw sugar is purified into white at a processing plant of this kind.

clue.text: Acceptable translation and transposition

parts.note: in means fashionable or acceptable
a version is a translation, as of a text

explanation.surface: A satisfactory translation that also moves words about.
explanation.definitionFit: Turning something upside down or reversing its order is a kind of transposing.

clue.text: Torrid run in up-to date surroundings

indicators.note: the run letter goes in the up-to-date word, which surrounds it

parts.note: topical means current or up to date
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: A hot run within modern surroundings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'surroundings' confirms the container: TOPICAL surrounds R.
explanation.definitionFit: Torrid weather is scorching, like that of the regions near the equator.

clue.text: Basic colours?

explanation.surface: A question about plain, ordinary colours.
explanation.definitionFit: Basic means ordinary or normal, and regimental colours are a flag, also called a banner carried by troops.

clue.text: She will shortly receive bill for varnish

indicators.note: the shortened pronoun and verb take in the bill, which is added at the end

parts.note: she will is shortened to she'll
AC, short for account, is a bill

explanation.surface: A woman who will soon be handed an invoice for wood finish.
explanation.definitionFit: A resin from the lac insect dissolved in alcohol is used as a wood finish.

clue.text: He made notes about tailless ark-dove

indicators.note: the remaining letters are moved about into a new order
the final letter of the hyphenated pair is cut off

explanation.surface: Noah's dove, missing its tail, being written about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tailless' removes the last E, leaving ARKDOV, and 'about' rearranges that to give the Czech composer.
explanation.definitionFit: Antonín Dvořák was a Czech composer, someone who wrote music.

clue.text: Matching Clement and Ruby, possibly

parts.note: clement means mild or kind
ruby is an example of the colour red

explanation.surface: Two people named Clement and Ruby who look alike.
explanation.walkthrough: Clement and Ruby look like names; one is an adjective for mild and the other a colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Similar in kind, like related spirits, is akin or matching.

clue.text: Thin slice of meat dipped in mescal, openly

indicators.note: the answer is dipped into the run of letters across these words

explanation.surface: A cutlet soaked in a Mexican spirit for all to see.
explanation.definitionFit: A thin boneless cutlet, often of veal, is beaten flat and fried.

clue.text: After a breather I need middle gear

indicators.note: the letter I comes after the breathing organ in the answer

parts.note: a lung is what one breathes with

explanation.surface: Someone who, after a break, needs a car's middle gear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'middle gear' suggests a car gearbox, but it is clothing worn round the middle: a lungi is a South Asian sarong-like wrap.
explanation.definitionFit: A cloth wrapped round the waist, worn in India and Burma, is clothing for the midriff.

clue.text: Norman's neighbour in British school

parts.note: Eton is the famous English public school

explanation.surface: A neighbour of someone called Norman who attends a British school.
explanation.walkthrough: Norman is not a man's name here: Brittany borders Normandy in France.
explanation.definitionFit: A person from Brittany lives next to Normandy, home of the Normans.

clue.text: Trout played by teacher

indicators.note: the fish is played with, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Schubert's Trout quintet being performed by a music teacher.
explanation.definitionFit: A private teacher coaches individual students.

clue.text: Retired county star

indicators.note: retiring means drawing back, so the county name is read backwards

parts.note: Avon was a former English county around Bristol

explanation.surface: A county's leading light has stepped down.
explanation.definitionFit: A star that suddenly flares brighter for a while is a nova.

clue.text: Lawn we keep private when it is dirty?

definitions.text: we keep private when it is dirty?

explanation.surface: Gardeners hiding a muddy lawn from the neighbours.
explanation.walkthrough: Lawn is a fine fabric, not grass; and the proverb says not to wash dirty linen in public.
explanation.definitionFit: Lawn is a fine cotton or flax fabric, and the saying warns against airing one's private scandals in public.

clue.text: Treble at Chester, for example?

parts.note: a treble is a boy soprano, such as one singing in Chester Cathedral's choir

explanation.surface: A triple helping of something in the city of Chester.
explanation.definitionFit: A boy soprano in a cathedral choir sings the top part.

clue.text: Off-colour, affected to be boorish

parts.note: off-colour means unwell or ill
mannered means affected or artificial in style

explanation.surface: Feeling unwell and putting on airs makes someone rude.
explanation.definitionFit: Rude and uncouth behaviour shows a lack of good breeding.
